title: Count messages and show the result
outcome: Calculate how many messages still need an answer.
story: Amina has 10 messages. Two new messages arrive, and she answers three. Help her keep the remaining count correct.

frames.explanation: The computer keeps the number under the name messages.
12 minus 3 makes 9. Amina still needs to answer nine messages.

sections.title: A name for a changing number
paragraphs: The shop needs a number it can update. A variable is a name a program uses to keep track of a value. In our example, messages is the name and 10 is its first value. When another message arrives, the name stays the same and the number becomes 11.
A familiar example is the score in a game. The score changes as you play. A program needs to remember the current score, rather than guess it from the screen. A message count works in the same way.

sections.title: Where the numbers come from
paragraphs: Input means information given to a program. We give our counter three inputs: the current count, the number of new messages, and the number Amina answered. Output means the result the program gives back. Here, the output is the remaining count.

For this first exercise, the lesson supplies those inputs. You only change the calculation. Later, an interface will collect inputs from a person, and a backend will load them from stored records. The calculation will still have the same job.

sections.title: Read the calculation in order
paragraphs: Start with 10. Add 2 to get 12. Subtract 3 to get 9. In JavaScript, + adds numbers and - subtracts them. We write current + incoming - answered to describe that process.

The equals sign in let remaining = current + incoming - answered stores the calculated result under the name remaining. Read the right side first, calculate its value, then connect that value to the name on the left. You do not need to memorise every symbol today.

sections.title: Check the result yourself
paragraphs: Before running the code, work out one example on paper. After running it, compare the output with your expected number. If you expected 9 and got 12, look for the instruction that subtracts answered messages.

Choose a second example too. If there are zero messages and zero new messages, the result should be zero. A working program should handle quiet days as well as busy days. The checks in the exercise try both situations.

words.meaning: A name used to keep track of a value.
The result the program returns or displays.

explanation: The first three lines give the program its input numbers.
The fourth line calculates 10 + 2 - 3 and keeps 9 under the name remaining.
console.log displays the value so you can check it. It does not save the number permanently.

exercise.title: Amina’s remaining-message counter
exercise.brief: The lesson provides current, incoming, and answered. Edit the line that calculates remaining. Start with new arrivals, then account for answered messages.

steps.title: Include new arrivals
steps.task: Change the calculation so incoming messages increase the current count.
steps.hint: Keep current and add incoming: current + incoming.

steps.title: Remove answered messages
steps.task: Now subtract answered messages. The same calculation must still handle a quiet day.
steps.hint: Read it as: old count + new arrivals - answered messages.

cases.label: 10 messages plus 2 arrivals
cases.why: New arrivals must increase the count.

cases.label: A quiet day
cases.why: Zero is a normal count, not a missing value.

cases.label: Three messages are answered
cases.why: The count tracks work still to do, not every message ever received.

cases.label: All messages are answered
cases.why: Finishing the queue should leave exactly zero.

project.title: A small message desk
project.brief: Make a calculation Amina can use to check the work left at the end of a shift. Use your completed exercise as the first version.
deliverables: A calculation using all three named inputs.
Two new examples with predicted and observed results.
A short explanation of what the output means.

milestones.title: Build the calculation
actions: Calculate remaining in one readable line.

milestones.title: Try another shift
actions: Predict the result for 8 current, 5 incoming, and 4 answered.
Run that case and compare it with your prediction.

milestones.title: Explain the work
actions: Name the three inputs and the output.
Describe what would happen if the subtraction were missing.

acceptance: Your new example has a recorded expected and actual result.
You can explain the calculation without reading the answer.
project.extension: Try a shift where Amina answers more messages than exist. Write down the problem you notice. Lesson 2 adds a rule to reject that input.
reflection: What information does the program need?
What did your extra example help you check?
